title: Soap Operas and Fertility: Evidence from Brazil
finding: Natural experiment (staggered entry of the Globo network, the main novela producer, across Brazilian markets): women in areas covered by Globo had significantly lower fertility per authors; effect strongest for lower-SES women and in central/late fertility phases, and not driven by selection in Globo entry. No effect size in the abstract.
why_for_us: Behaviour shifts when a desirable way of life is simply shown as normal in the story world (small families were never 'pitched'); show the office using the tool as background normality rather than arguing for it.

title: Television and Divorce: Evidence from Brazilian Novelas
venue: Journal of the European Economic Association
finding: Natural experiment (timing of Globo signal availability, census 1970/1980/1991, area fixed effects): the share of separated or divorced women rose significantly after the signal arrived per authors; stronger in smaller areas where the signal reached a larger share of the population.
why_for_us: Effect scales with share of the community exposed: in a small profession like notaries, reach within the peer group matters more than raw view counts.

title: The Power of TV: Cable Television and Women's Status in India
finding: Three-year individual-level panel (quasi-experimental, rural India): introduction of cable TV was associated with significant decreases in reported acceptability of domestic violence and son preference, increased women's autonomy and lower fertility per authors; results argued not to be driven by pre-existing trends.
why_for_us: Exposure to 'other ways of doing things' on screen moves attitudes even without an explicit message; depict a credible alternative office routine and let viewers compare it with their own.

title: Media Influences on Social Outcomes: The Impact of MTV's 16 and Pregnant on Teen Childbearing
finding: Instrumental-variables design (pre-period local MTV ratings predicting show ratings): per authors the show led to a 4.3 percent reduction in teen births. Note: the identification was publicly disputed (Jaeger, Joyce & Kaestner 2016, SSRN, indexed in OpenAlex without abstract).
why_for_us: Showing realistic costs and consequences of the status quo can move behaviour, but this headline effect is contested; do not cite it as settled proof in pitch material.

title: The Entertaining Way to Behavioral Change: Fighting HIV with MTV
finding: RCT in urban Nigeria (MTV Shuga vs placebo TV series): significant gains in HIV knowledge and attitudes; treated viewers were twice as likely to get tested for HIV eight months later per authors, with fewer STDs among women. Effects were stronger for viewers more involved with the narrative; added social-norm manipulations produced no extra effect.
why_for_us: Narrative involvement is the active ingredient and a concrete low-cost action (testing = a free trial) is the outcome that moves; build each arc toward one small doable step and do not rely on bolted-on 'everyone does it' messaging.

title: Reducing intergroup prejudice and conflict using the media: A field experiment in Rwanda
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Year-long field experiment (reconciliation radio soap vs health radio soap control): listeners' perceptions of social norms and their behaviours changed (intermarriage, open dissent, trust, cooperation), but the programme did little to change personal beliefs per author; group discussion and emotion were implicated in the process.
why_for_us: Serial drama changes what people think their peers do before it changes what they privately believe; write to make tool use look like the norm among respected notaries and make episodes easy to discuss in the office.

title: Harnessing Emotional Connections to Improve Financial Decisions: Evaluating the Impact of Financial Education in Mainstream Media
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 6407 (published version: JEEA 2017, W3121730031, no abstract in OpenAlex)
finding: Randomised symmetric encouragement design, South African soap 'Scandal!' with a two-month debt storyline vs a comparison soap: higher financial knowledge, viewers almost twice as likely to borrow from formal sources, less gambling and hire-purchase per authors. Messages promoting a debt helpline delivered by an external character did not sustain traction beyond immediate interest; focus groups point to emotional connection with the leading character.
why_for_us: Put the product behaviour in the hands of a lead character viewers already care about, across several episodes; a guest 'expert' or brand voice delivering the call to action is the part that failed.

title: Effects of an Entertainment-education Radio Soap Opera on Family Planning Behavior in Tanzania
finding: Field experiment (soap broadcast by seven Radio Tanzania stations, one comparison area 1993-95; five annual surveys of about 2,750 households plus clinic data from 79 clinics): strong behavioural effects on family planning adoption per authors, via increased self-efficacy and more talk with spouses and peers. No effect size in the abstract.
why_for_us: Self-efficacy ('I could do this too') and conversation with peers are the pathways; show the first use of the tool as easy and give staff a line worth repeating to a colleague.

title: East Los High: Transmedia Edutainment to Promote the Sexual and Reproductive Health of Young Latina/o Americans
finding: Mixed evaluation of season 1 (online analytics 2013-14, viewer survey, lab experiment): wide reach, strong viewer engagement and positive cognitive, emotional and social impact per authors; no effect sizes in the abstract, and the design is weaker than the RCTs in this register.
why_for_us: Precedent for a streaming-native series whose educational content lives in the story and whose resources sit on companion platforms; keep the how-to detail in linked material, not in the episode.

title: Economic and Social Impacts of the Media
venue: NBER Working Paper (chapter version: Handbook of Media Economics, W1932359374)
finding: Review of causal media-effects studies across education, family choices, health, consumption and savings: the authors stress that demand for entertainment plays the key role, with economic and social impacts emerging largely as by-products of entertainment consumption.
why_for_us: The audience comes for the story, and the impact is a by-product; an episode that is not worth watching on its own merits has no channel through which to teach anything.

title: The effectiveness of using entertainment education narratives to promote safer sexual behaviors of youth: A meta-analysis, 1985-2017
finding: Meta-analysis (k=10: eight experimental, two quasi-experimental; N=23,476): small behavioural effects per authors (unprotected sex SMD=0.08; number of partners SMD=0.17; STI testing SMD=0.29), medium effect on knowledge (SMD=0.67) with a time-decay relationship, and no effects on attitudes.
why_for_us: Expect knowledge gains that fade and small behaviour effects; plan recurring exposure (seasons, recaps) and measure trial sign-ups, not stated attitudes.

title: Effectiveness of entertainment education in communicating health information: a systematic review
finding: Meta-analysis (k=22, N=19,517): entertainment-education had a small but significant overall effect on knowledge, attitudes, intentions and behaviours, average r=.12 per authors.
why_for_us: Calibrates expectations: a realistic effect is small per viewer, so the business case depends on reach within the profession and on repetition.

title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of Entertainment-Education interventions on persuasive health outcomes
finding: Meta-analysis of controlled or randomised-controlled studies only (K=39 of 4,183 screened): significant small-to-moderate effects on knowledge, intentions, attitudes, behaviour and self-efficacy, largest for knowledge and self-efficacy per authors; substantial heterogeneity, authors urge caution.
why_for_us: The most reliable gains are 'I know how it works' and 'I could do it'; write episodes that demonstrate one concrete step of the workflow so the viewer leaves able to picture doing it.

title: Toward a Theory of Entertainment Persuasion: Explaining the Persuasive Effects of Entertainment-Education Messages
finding: Theoretical article: separates identification, parasocial interaction, similarity and related constructs, synthesises existing E-E processing theories and advances propositions on how involvement with storyline and characters lets entertainment messages persuade where overt appeals meet resistance.
why_for_us: Gives the writers' room a checklist per episode: which character carries identification, which carries liking, and which form of audience resistance the scene is meant to lower.

title: Entertainment-Education and Elaboration Likelihood: Understanding the Processing of Narrative Persuasion
finding: Theoretical review (extended ELM): absorption in a narrative and response to characters should enhance persuasion and suppress counterarguing when the implicit persuasive content is counterattitudinal, and classic moderators such as topic involvement should matter less; supporting evidence is reviewed.
why_for_us: Keep the persuasive content implicit and inside the plot; the moment the viewer steps out of the story to evaluate a claim, the sceptical legal mind is back in charge.

title: Social Cognitive Theory for Personal and Social Change by Enabling Media
finding: Book chapter by Albert Bandura in the Singhal et al. volume, setting out the social cognitive / social modelling basis of the entertainment-education strategy; the OpenAlex record carries only an author note, no abstract.
why_for_us: Reference text for the modelling logic behind positive, negative and transitional characters; consult the chapter itself before designing the cast.

title: Miguel Sabido's Entertainment-Education
finding: Practitioner chapter by Sabido describing his methodology: begin with a theoretical framework and a testable hypothesis, use production and direction techniques to create intended tones, then evaluate whether the initiative worked; includes examples up to recent online work.
why_for_us: Treat each season as a hypothesis with a pre-agreed measure (e.g. demo requests from viewers), and decide the tone of each scene deliberately rather than by default.

title: A Staged Model of Communication Effects: Evidence from an Entertainment-Education Radio Soap Opera in Tanzania
finding: Synthesises hierarchy-of-effects, stages-of-change, social learning theory and diffusion of innovations into a staged model in which messages change behaviour by stimulating (1) involvement with media characters and role modelling of their actions and (2) interpersonal communication; tested on Tanzanian field-experiment data.
why_for_us: Plan the season as stages (awareness, liking a character, seeing the action modelled, talking about it, trying it) and give each episode one stage to serve.

title: Reinforcement or Reactance? Examining the Effect of an Explicit Persuasive Appeal Following an Entertainment-Education Narrative
finding: Experiment on a TV drama about drinking and driving with or without an explicit persuasive appeal (epilogue): narrative and explicit appeal interacted in their effect on attitudes per authors; the abstract does not state the direction of the interaction.
why_for_us: An end-card call to action is not neutral: it can reinforce or trigger reactance depending on the story before it, so A/B test episodes with and without an explicit product tag.

title: The Effect of Similarity to a Transitional Role Model of an Entertainment-Education Narrative Designed to Improve Attitudes Toward Immigrants: Evidence from Three European Countries
finding: Three parallel online experiments (Greece N=286, Italy N=295, Spain N=294): demographic similarity to a transitional protagonist raised perceived similarity and, in turn, identification; identification was associated with more cognitive elaboration and meaningful affect, which were associated with more positive attitudes in all three countries (indirect effects).
why_for_us: The sceptic-who-changes should look like the target viewer: a notary or senior clerk of similar age and office type, not a young tech enthusiast.

title: Meta-analytic evidence for the persuasive effect of narratives on beliefs, attitudes, intentions, and behaviors
finding: Meta-analysis: exposure to a narrative relates positively to narrative-consistent beliefs (k=37, r=.17), attitudes (k=40, r=.19), intentions (k=28, r=.17) and behaviours (k=5, r=.23) per authors; fictionality moderator mixed, medium and research design did not matter, unidentified moderators remain.
why_for_us: Fiction persuades about as well as fact-based narrative and the medium is not the lever; invest in story quality rather than worrying that an invented office undermines the message.

title: Impact of Narratives on Persuasion in Health Communication: A Meta-Analysis
finding: Meta-analysis (k=25, N=9,330): narratives had a small overall effect on persuasion (r=.063) per authors; audio and video narratives produced significant effects while print did not; narratives advocating detection and prevention behaviours worked, those advocating cessation did not.
why_for_us: Video is the right carrier, and 'start doing this' is easier to sell by story than 'stop doing that'; frame episodes around adopting a new step, not abandoning the old habit.

title: The Extended Transportation-Imagery Model: A Meta-Analysis of the Antecedents and Consequences of Consumers' Narrative Transportation
finding: Meta-analysis of 132 effect sizes from 76 articles testing a model of storyteller, story and story-receiver antecedents of narrative transportation and its consequences for consumers; the abstract reports the model and corpus but no pooled effect sizes.
why_for_us: Use the full paper's antecedent list (identifiable characters, imaginable plot, verisimilitude) as a script-review rubric; the abstract alone does not give thresholds.

title: The Effects of Engagement with Entertainment
venue: Annals of the International Communication Association
finding: Meta-analysis of involvement with entertainment media (homophily, empathic identification, parasocial relationships, transportation): media involvement is moderately associated with persuasive outcomes (r=.27) per authors; message content domain moderated the effect.
why_for_us: Involvement with characters is the strongest correlate of persuasion in this register; recurring characters across eight episodes are an asset worth protecting from one-off gag formats.

title: The role of transportation in the persuasiveness of public narratives
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Experiments (Exp. 1 N=97; Exp. 2 N=69): the extent of transportation into a story increased story-consistent beliefs and favourable evaluations of protagonists, and highly transported readers found fewer 'false notes' in the story than less-transported readers.
why_for_us: A transported viewer stops fact-checking; the first seconds must pull the viewer into a recognisable office situation before any product-relevant beat appears.

title: Explaining the Effects of Narrative in an Entertainment Television Program: Overcoming Resistance to Persuasion
finding: Between-subjects experiment (N=367 undergraduates; dramatic narrative vs non-narrative programme; immediate and 2-week measures): the drama reduced reactance by fostering parasocial interaction and lowering perceived persuasive intent; identification reduced counterarguing; unexpectedly, transportation was associated with more counterarguing.
why_for_us: Liking a character and not feeling sold to are what lower resistance; absorption alone is not enough, so keep any visible selling intent out of the scene.

title: Overcoming Resistance Through Narratives: Findings from a Meta-Analytic Review
finding: Two-part meta-analysis: narratives generated less resistance than non-narratives (9 experiments, 15 effect sizes, d=-.213); narrative engagement correlated negatively with resistance (25 studies, 63 effect sizes, r=-.131), moderated by genre, length, medium and character unit per authors.
why_for_us: The resistance-reduction effect is real but small and depends on format features including length; test whether 60-90 s gives enough engagement or whether the arc must carry across episodes.

title: Long-term Persuasive Effects in Narrative Communication Research: A Meta-Analysis
finding: Meta-analysis (14 studies; 51 immediate and 66 delayed effect sizes): a single narrative message had a stronger impact than a non-narrative one on attitudes and intentions immediately and on attitudes, intentions and behaviours at delayed measurement; no difference for beliefs; transportation mediated the immediate effects.
why_for_us: The narrative advantage survives a delay, which suits a long B2B decision cycle; do not expect the story to out-teach a plain explainer on factual beliefs.

title: Persuasive Effects of Fictional Narratives Increase Over Time
finding: Experiment (N=81; fictional story containing true and false assertions vs control story): large short-term persuasive effects of false information, even larger after a two-week delay (absolute sleeper effect); belief certainty dipped immediately and returned to baseline after two weeks.
why_for_us: What the drama shows about how the tool works will be remembered as fact weeks later, including errors; every depicted feature, deadline and legal step must be accurate.

title: The Differential Impact of Statistical and Narrative Evidence on Beliefs, Attitude, and Intention: A Meta-Analysis
finding: Meta-analysis: statistical evidence had a stronger influence than narrative evidence on beliefs and attitude, whereas narrative evidence had a stronger influence on intention per authors (no pooled coefficients in the abstract).
why_for_us: Split the work: the drama builds the intention to try, while numbers (time saved, error rates) belong on the landing page or end card where the analytical reader looks for them.

title: “Hey, that could be me”: The role of similarity in narrative persuasion
finding: Experiment (N=582; 324 students, 258 older adults): age similarity to the protagonist, where relevant to the story topic, raised identification, transportation and donation intention, but only among students; for older adults protagonist age or gender made almost no difference; perceived similarity related to transportation and identification in SEM.
why_for_us: Demographic matching is not a guaranteed lever for mature viewers; similarity of situation (the same deadlines, clients and paperwork) is the safer route to 'that could be me'.

title: Identification With Characters, Elaboration, and Counterarguing in Entertainment-Education Interventions Through Audiovisual Fiction
finding: Experiment (N=208, ages 14-20, randomly assigned to one of three episodes of a Colombian E-E series): greater identification with the main character was associated with more cognitive elaboration, which led to more favourable attitudes; counterarguing did not play a significant mediating role. Authors conclude characters can make explicit arguments in dialogue.
why_for_us: For an audience that likes to reason, a character the viewer identifies with may voice a real argument in dialogue; thinking along is a route to persuasion, not a threat to it.

title: Teaching Through Television: Experimental Evidence on Entrepreneurship Education in Tanzania
finding: Randomised field experiment (more than 2,000 secondary students incentivised to watch an edutainment show over almost three months): only suggestive evidence of greater interest in business; the main finding per authors is negative, with a strong negative effect on school performance, fewer continuing schooling long-term, and little evidence of more business ownership.
why_for_us: A show can shift aspirations in a direction nobody intended; check what else the episodes implicitly devalue (for example careful manual review) and measure side effects, not only the target outcome.

title: Entertainment-Education in the Context of Humor: Effects on Safer Sex Intentions and Risk Perceptions
finding: Experiment (same pregnancy storyline with vs without related humour): humour reduced counterarguing but trivialised the severity of consequences; in the original humorous version viewers reported greater intentions to engage in unprotected sex than in the serious-tone version.
why_for_us: Do not make the joke about the risk itself (a document error, a missed deadline): comedy lowers defences but also makes the problem the tool solves feel unimportant.

title: A Priest, a Rabbi, and a Minister Walk into a Bar: A Meta-Analysis of Humor Effects on Persuasion
finding: Meta-analysis (89 studies): humour has a weak overall effect on persuasion (r=.13), moderate on knowledge (r=.23), weak on attitudes (r=.12) and behavioural intent (r=.09); related humour works better for highly involved individuals; inverted U-shaped effect of humour intensity; no humour sleeper effect.
why_for_us: Use moderate humour that grows out of the office work itself (the viewers are highly involved); broad or heavy comedy sits on the wrong side of the inverted U.

title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Disclosing Sponsored Content
finding: Meta-analysis (61 papers, 57 data sets): disclosing sponsored content reduced brand attitudes, credibility and source evaluation and increased recognition, persuasion knowledge and resistance per authors; disclosure content, timing and awareness are boundary conditions.
why_for_us: The brand origin must be disclosed anyway, and the cost is known; pay it once and plainly (channel identity, end card) instead of letting viewers discover mid-episode that the story is an advert.

title: Using Eye Tracking to Understand the Effects of Brand Placement Disclosure Types in Television Programs
finding: Eye-tracking experiment (N=149): a text disclosure combined with a product-placement logo was most effective at making viewers recognise advertising, a logo alone least effective; the effect was mediated by visual attention to the disclosure (abstract truncated in the search record; brand-response results not read).
why_for_us: How noticeable the sponsor cue is determines whether persuasion knowledge switches on; decide deliberately where and how large the brand mark sits in a vertical frame.

title: The Persuasion Knowledge Model: How People Cope with Persuasion Attempts
finding: Theoretical model of how people develop and use knowledge about persuasion agents' goals and tactics to cope with persuasion attempts, including how consumers use selling attempts to refine attitudes toward the product and toward the marketer.
why_for_us: Lawyers have unusually developed persuasion knowledge; assume they will identify the tactic, so the story must still be worth their time once they have recognised it as marketing.

title: Fictionality and Perceived Realism in Experiencing Stories: A Model of Narrative Comprehension and Engagement
finding: Theoretical model with reviewed evidence: fictionality itself does not affect narrative processing, but violations of external realism (match with the real world) and narrative realism (internal coherence) may trigger negative realism evaluations, disrupt engagement and lessen a narrative's persuasive power.
why_for_us: Notaries will forgive invented people but not a wrong procedure, an impossible deadline or an AI-video glitch in a document; one professional false note breaks the episode, so have a practising notary vet every script.

title: Perceived Realism: Dimensions and Roles in Narrative Persuasion
finding: Survey-experimental data on messages on three topics: perceived realism has five dimensions (plausibility, typicality, factuality, narrative consistency, perceptual quality); plausibility predicted emotional involvement, typicality predicted identification, narrative consistency and perceptual quality predicted message evaluation, and these in turn predicted attitudes.
why_for_us: Typical cases (an ordinary sale deed on a busy Friday) drive identification better than spectacular ones, and perceptual quality feeds message evaluation, so visible AI-video artefacts cost persuasion.

title: Transportation Into Narrative Worlds: The Role of Prior Knowledge and Perceived Realism
finding: Correlational study (N=152 undergraduates reading one story): transportation correlated positively with perceived realism; readers with prior knowledge or experience relevant to the story themes were more transported; transported readers held more story-consistent beliefs, with or without prior experience.
why_for_us: Insider knowledge is an asset when the depiction rings true: accurate office detail should deepen transportation among notaries rather than bore them.

title: The effectiveness of case-based learning in health professional education. A BEME systematic review: BEME Guide No. 23
finding: Systematic review with narrative synthesis (104 papers, 23 rated higher quality; mostly single-cohort, post-only evaluations): students and teachers overwhelmingly enjoy case-based learning and believe it enhances learning, but the empirical data taken as a whole are inconclusive on learning effects compared with other activities.
why_for_us: Professionals like learning from cases, yet liking is not evidence of learning; do not treat positive comments on episodes as proof that viewers understood how the tool fits the workflow.

title: Comparison of text and video cases in a postgraduate problem-based learning format
finding: Small comparative study (11 paediatric residents in two groups; a 2.5-minute video of a patient case vs an equivalent written description): verbal interaction showed statistically significant improvements in data exploration, theory building and theory evaluation after the video case.
why_for_us: A case shown in about two and a half minutes of video sharpened professional reasoning more than the same case in text; the micro-drama length is not too short to stimulate professional thinking. Very small sample.

title: Narrative medicine as a medical education tool: A systematic review
finding: Systematic review (36 articles, BEME and Kirkpatrick scales): positive measurable impact on participation, attitudes, knowledge and skills, but unequivocal evidence of an effect on behaviour or on ongoing interaction with colleagues and patients is still lacking per authors.
why_for_us: With professional audiences, stories reliably move attitudes and knowledge while behaviour change is unproven; pair the series with a concrete trial path instead of expecting the drama alone to produce adoption.

title: Local opinion leaders: effects on professional practice and health care outcomes
finding: Cochrane review of RCTs (18 studies, more than 296 hospitals and 318 primary-care practitioners): across studies the median adjusted risk difference was +0.12, a 12% absolute increase in compliance with desired practice; effects ranged from a 15% decrease to a 72% increase and the opinion leader's role was mostly poorly described.
why_for_us: Respected peers measurably shift professional practice; the model character should read as a credible senior colleague, and real notaries endorsing or appearing around the series add a tested mechanism.

title: Innovation characteristics and innovation adoption-implementation: A meta-analysis of findings
finding: Review and meta-analysis of 75 articles: three innovation characteristics (compatibility, relative advantage and complexity) had the most consistent significant relationship to innovation adoption.
why_for_us: Each episode should dramatise one of three things: the tool fits how the office already works, it is clearly better than the current way, and it is not complicated.

title: “AI Am Here to Represent You”: Understanding How Institutional Logics Shape Attitudes Toward Intelligent Technologies in Legal Work
finding: Qualitative study (30 semi-structured interviews with lawyers, law librarians, paralegals, document clerks and law students): three institutional logics (expertise, accessibility, efficiency) guide how legal workers understand and use AI; they hold contradictory attitudes, and occupational role shapes the stance.
why_for_us: Write the ambivalence in: the notary guarding expertise and the clerk wanting efficiency are both true to life, and the plot should resolve their tension by keeping expertise with the human.

title: Adopting robot lawyer? The extending artificial intelligence robot lawyer technology acceptance model for legal industry by an exploratory study
finding: Exploratory semi-structured interviews with lawyers, judges, AI experts and potential clients, yielding an extended acceptance model with two highlighted dimensions, 'legal use' and 'perception of trust'; authors conclude AI must work together with human lawyers. No quantitative test.
why_for_us: Show the assistant drafting and the notary deciding; any scene where the software appears to replace professional judgement hits the trust dimension head-on.

title: Exemplification Theory: Judging the Whole by Some of Its Parts
finding: Theoretical essay giving a conceptual foundation for exemplification: how individual cases presented in communication shape judgements about the wider population of cases (search-record abstract truncated; no empirical figures read).
why_for_us: The one office in the series will be taken as representative of 'offices that use this tool'; choose the exemplar (size, town, type of work) to match the segment we want to feel addressed.

title: The Hollywood Robot Syndrome: Media Effects on Older Adults' Attitudes toward Robots and Adoption Intentions
venue: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction (HRI)
finding: Survey with SEM (N=379, mean age 66): the more media portrayals of robots respondents recalled, the lower their anxiety toward robots, which fed perceived usefulness, ease of use and adoption intentions; recalling human-like or sympathy-eliciting robots related to more positive attitudes. Correlational.
why_for_us: Familiarity through fiction lowers technology anxiety, and a sympathetic depiction helps; give the assistant a consistent, likeable on-screen presence across episodes.

title: The CSI Effect: Popular Fiction About Forensic Science Affects the Public's Expectations About Real Forensic Science
finding: Mock-juror study with a simulated trial transcript: CSI viewers were more critical of the forensic evidence and found it less believable than non-viewers; 18% of CSI viewers vs 29% of non-viewers would convict (not statistically significant); viewers of general crime shows did not differ.
why_for_us: Glamorised fiction raises expectations that the real thing then fails to meet; never show the tool doing more, faster or more flawlessly than the product does.

title: Television Viewing and Public Perceptions of Attorneys
finding: Content analysis plus survey (cultivation design): prime-time depictions of attorneys affect public perceptions of attorneys, especially their front-region behaviours; content-specific viewing predicts this better than total viewing or sociodemographics.
why_for_us: Genre-specific viewing shapes how a legal profession is seen; notaries will judge the series first on how it portrays them, so the notary must never be the fool of the piece.

title: Media Use, Interpersonal Communication, and Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence
finding: Nationally representative online panel survey (US): respondents framed AI as social progress or as Pandora's box; technology news use predicted change in support for AI, while science-fiction viewing and discussing technology were only conditionally related to such change.
why_for_us: Fiction's effect on AI attitudes is conditional, not automatic; viewers arrive with a 'Pandora's box' frame available, so the script should answer loss-of-control worries inside the story (who checks, who signs).
